topic.angle: Kitty Genovese and what the research really says

panels.text: 1964, Queens, New York. Two weeks after Kitty Genovese was murdered, a newspaper reported that thirty-seven witnesses saw or heard it and none helped.

Psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané brought the topic into the lab. In one 1969 study by Latané and Judith Rodin, 70% of people alone called out or went to help a woman who seemed hurt, but only 40% did when paired with a stranger.
The famous story was exaggerated. Some neighbours heard cries but many did not realise how serious it was, and her friend Sophia Farrar held her until an ambulance arrived.
The effect itself is real but nuanced. A 2011 meta-analysis found it most likely in non-dangerous emergencies, and not in dangerous ones.

probes.question: True or false: later investigations showed the original newspaper account of the Genovese murder was exaggerated.
In a 2011 meta-analysis, when was the bystander effect most likely to occur?
options: Only when the victim was a friend

claims.claim: 1964, Queens: two weeks after Genovese was murdered a newspaper reported thirty-seven witnesses saw or heard it and none helped
claims.quote: Two weeks after the murder, The New York Times published an article claiming that thirty-seven witnesses saw or heard the attack

claims.claim: Darley and Latane brought the topic into the lab
claims.quote: first demonstrated and popularized in the laboratory by social psychologists John M. Darley and Bibb Latané in 1968

claims.claim: In one 1969 study by Latane and Judith Rodin, 70% of people alone called out or went to help a woman who seemed hurt, only 40% when paired with a stranger
claims.quote: Seventy percent of the people alone called out or went to help the woman after they believed she had fallen and was hurt

claims.claim: ...but only 40% did when paired with a stranger
claims.quote: but when paired with a stranger only 40 percent offered help

claims.claim: Later investigations showed the story was exaggerated (probe 1)
claims.quote: However, subsequent investigations revealed that the extent of public apathy was exaggerated.

claims.claim: Some neighbours heard cries but many did not realise how serious it was
claims.quote: While some neighbors heard her cries, many did not realize the severity of the situation.

claims.claim: Friend Sophia Farrar held her until an ambulance arrived
claims.quote: held her in her arms, whispering, "Help is on the way" until an ambulance arrived
one of the strongest and most replicable effects in social psychology

claims.claim: 2011 meta-analysis: most likely in non-dangerous emergencies, not in dangerous ones (probe 2)
claims.quote: A 2011 meta-analysis found that the bystander effect was most likely to occur in non-dangerous emergencies but did not occur in dangerous emergencies.
